Reading · how animals adapt

1.1 Discuss. Which animals could survive if the climate where you live changed completely? Which would disappear first?

KEY WORDS

a specialist suited to one narrow set of conditions

a generalist able to live in many conditions

to tolerate to survive something difficult

to indicate to be a sign of something

Life at the Edges

There is almost nowhere on Earth without something living in it. If you drill three kilometres down into solid rock, you find bacteria. If you lower a camera into the deepest trench in the Pacific, something swims past it. Life does not merely tolerate extreme conditions; in a surprising number of cases it appears to prefer them.

The Antarctic icefish is a useful example. Its blood contains no red cells at all, which in any other vertebrate would be fatal. Instead it produces a protein that stops ice crystals forming, and it absorbs oxygen straight through skin so thin that the animal looks almost transparent. If the water around it warms by more than a couple of degrees, the icefish dies. It has adapted so precisely that it can no longer adapt again.

That is the uncomfortable part of the story. Specialisation is efficient, and efficiency is dangerous. A generalist — a rat, a crow, a human being — survives change precisely because it was never very good at any one thing. If conditions shift, it moves, eats something else and carries on. The icefish has no such option.

Biologists worry less about the loss of any individual species than about what that loss indicates. When a specialist disappears, it is usually because the conditions it depended on have gone. If those conditions keep changing at the present rate, the animals that survive will be the ones we find least appealing: the adaptable, the ordinary, the ones already living in our cities.

2

Grammar · zero and first conditionals

PRESENTATION

ZERO conditional — a general truth or a scientific fact. Both clauses are present simple, and if means when:

If you heat ice, it melts. · When water freezes, it expands.

FIRST conditional — one real possibility in the future: if + present simple, will / won't + infinitive:

If the water warms, the icefish will die.

Also: may · might · could · should instead of will · unless = if … not · present simple after when, as soon as, until, provided that.

Zero — always true

First — one future possibility

If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

If you heat that pan, it will boil in a minute.

If it rains, the river rises.

If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel the trip.

Ice melts if the temperature rises.

The ice will melt if it gets any warmer.

Plants die if they don't get water.

The plants will die unless you water them.

ERROR WARNING

Never use will in the if-clause:

If it will rain, we'll stay in. ✗ If it rains, we'll stay in. ✓

unless already means if not — do not add a second negative:

Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late. ✗ Unless you hurry, you'll be late. ✓

The clauses can swap round. When if comes second, there is no comma: We'll stay in if it rains.

Everyday English · giving yourself time to think

4.1 Read the conversation.

Aziz What do you think is the biggest environmental problem here?

Malika That's a good question. Let me think for a moment.

Aziz Take your time.

Malika Well, I suppose it depends what you mean by biggest.

Aziz Say, the one that affects the most people.

Malika In that case, water. Or rather, the lack of it.

Aziz Yes, I'd say exactly the same.

Buying time

Narrowing the question

Correcting yourself

That's a good question.

It depends what you mean by…

Or rather, …

Let me think for a moment.

In what sense exactly?

What I mean is…

I've never thought about that.

If you mean … , then …

Actually, let me rephrase that.

ERROR WARNING

These phrases must sound natural, not memorised. Two per conversation is plenty.

It depends on what you mean from that. ✗ It depends what you mean by that. ✓ · How to say…? ✗ What's the word…? ✓
